title: How to hear this sermon
english: This is a listening version of John Wesley's sermon, The Witness of Our Own Spirit. It is the sermon as printed in John Wesley's 1771 Works. The printing gives no preach date. Rendered in modern English.

This is our rejoicing, the testimony of our conscience: that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have lived our manner of life in the world. 2 Corinthians 1:12.

title: The testimony of our conscience
english: Such is the voice of every true believer in Christ, so long as he abides in faith and love. The one who follows me, says our Lord, does not walk in darkness (John 8:12). And while he has the light, he rejoices in it. As he has received the Lord Jesus Christ, so he walks in him. And while he walks in him, the apostle's exhortation takes hold in his soul day by day: Rejoice in the Lord always, and again I say, rejoice (Philippians 4:4).

But so that we do not build our house upon the sand, lest when the rains come down, and the winds blow, and the floods rise and beat upon it, it fall, and great is the fall of it, I intend in the following discourse to show what the nature and ground of a Christian's joy are. We know, in general, that it is that happy peace, that calm satisfaction of spirit, which arises from such a testimony of his conscience as the apostle describes here. But to understand this more thoroughly, we must weigh all his words. From that it will easily appear both what we are to understand by conscience, and what by the testimony of it, and also how the one who has this testimony rejoices evermore.

title: What conscience is
english: And first, what are we to understand by conscience? What is the meaning of this word that is in everyone's mouth? One would imagine it was an extremely difficult thing to discover, when we consider how large and numerous volumes have been written on this subject from time to time, and how all the treasures of ancient and modern learning have been ransacked in order to explain it. And yet it is to be feared that it has not received much light from all those elaborate inquiries. Rather, have not most of those writers confused the matter, darkening counsel by words without knowledge (Job 38:2), and perplexed a subject that is plain in itself and easy to understand? Set aside the hard words, and every person of an honest heart will soon understand the thing.

God has made us thinking beings, able to perceive what is present, and to reflect or look back on what is past. In particular, we are able to perceive whatever passes in our own hearts or lives, to know whatever we feel or do, and that either while it passes or when it is past. This is what we mean when we say that a person is a conscious being. He has a consciousness, or inward perception, both of things present and past that relate to himself, of his own tempers and outward behavior. But what we usually call conscience implies something more than this. It is not merely the knowledge of our present life, or the memory of the life that went before. To remember, to bear witness either of past or present things, is only one office of conscience, and the least. Its main business is to excuse or accuse, to approve or disapprove, to acquit or condemn.

Some recent writers have given a new name to this, and have chosen to call it a moral sense. But the old word seems preferable to the new, if only for this reason, that it is more common and familiar among people, and therefore easier to understand. And to Christians it is undeniably preferable on another account also, namely, because it is scriptural, because it is the word which the wisdom of God has chosen to use in the inspired writings.

And according to the meaning in which it is generally used there, particularly in the epistles of Saint Paul, we may understand by conscience a faculty or power, implanted by God in every soul that comes into the world, of perceiving what is right or wrong in one's own heart or life, in one's tempers, thoughts, words, and actions.

title: The rule of right and wrong
english: But what is the rule by which people are to judge of right and wrong? By what is their conscience to be directed? The rule of the heathens, as the apostle teaches elsewhere, is the law written in their hearts (Romans 2:15). These, he says, not having the outward law, are a law to themselves. They show the work of the law, that which the outward law prescribes, written in their heart by the finger of God. Their conscience also bears witness whether they walk by this rule or not, and their thoughts meanwhile accuse them, or else excuse them, acquit them, and defend them. Romans 2:14-15.

But the Christian rule of right and wrong is the word of God, the writings of the Old and New Testament. It is all that the prophets and holy men of old wrote as they were moved by the Holy Ghost, and all that scripture which was given by inspiration of God. And it is indeed profitable for doctrine, or teaching the whole will of God; for reproof of what is contrary to it; for correction of error; and for instruction, or training us up, in righteousness. 2 Timothy 3:16.

This is a lantern to a Christian's feet, and a light in all his paths. This alone he receives as his rule of right or wrong, of whatever is really good or evil. He counts nothing good but what is commanded here, either directly or by plain consequence. He counts nothing evil but what is forbidden here, either in express terms or by an undeniable inference. Whatever the scripture neither forbids nor commands, either directly or by plain consequence, he believes to be of an indifferent nature, in itself neither good nor evil. This is the whole and sole outward rule by which his conscience is to be directed in all things.

title: A conscience void of offense
english: And if it is in fact directed by that rule, then he has the answer of a good conscience toward God. A good conscience is what the apostle elsewhere calls a conscience void of offense. So what he at one time expresses thus, I have lived in all good conscience before God until this day, Acts 23:1, he means at another time by that expression, In this I exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offense toward God and toward man, Acts 24:16.

Now, in order to this, there is absolutely required, first, a right understanding of the word of God, of his holy and acceptable and perfect will concerning us, as it is revealed there. For it is impossible that we should walk by a rule if we do not know what it means.

There is required, second, and how few have reached it, a true knowledge of ourselves: a knowledge both of our hearts and lives, of our inward tempers and outward manner of life. For if we do not know them, it is not possible that we should compare them with our rule.

There is required, third, an agreement of our hearts and lives, of our tempers and manner of life, of our thoughts and words and works, with that rule, with the written word of God. For without this, if we have any conscience at all, it can be only an evil conscience.

There is required, fourth, an inward perception of this agreement with our rule. And this habitual perception, this inward consciousness itself, is properly a good conscience, or, in the apostle's other phrase, a conscience void of offense toward God and toward man.

title: No other foundation than Jesus Christ
english: But whoever desires to have a conscience thus void of offense, let him see that he lays the right foundation. Let him remember that no one can lay any other foundation for this than that which is laid, even Jesus Christ. And let him also remember that no one builds on him except by a living faith, and that no one is a partaker of Christ until he can clearly testify, The life which I now live, I live by faith in the Son of God, in him who is now revealed in my heart, who loved me and gave himself for me.

Faith alone is that evidence, that conviction, that demonstration of things invisible, by which, the eyes of our understanding being opened and divine light poured in upon them, we see the wondrous things of God's law, its excellency and its purity, its height and depth and length and breadth, and of every commandment contained in it. It is by faith that, beholding the light of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ, we perceive, as in a mirror, all that is in ourselves, yes, the inmost motions of our souls. And by this alone can that blessed love of God be shed abroad in our hearts, which enables us to love one another as Christ loved us.

By this is that gracious promise fulfilled to all the Israel of God: I will put my laws into their minds, and write them, or engrave them, in their hearts. Hebrews 8:10. By this he produces in their souls an entire agreement with his holy and perfect law, and brings into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ.

And as an evil tree cannot bring forth good fruit, so a good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit. As the heart of a believer, so likewise his life, is thoroughly conformed to the rule of God's commandments. Conscious of that, he can give glory to God and say with the apostle, This is our rejoicing, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have lived our manner of life in the world.

title: One word for the whole of life
english: We have lived our manner of life. The apostle expresses this in the original by one single word. But the meaning of it is extremely broad. It takes in our whole conduct, yes, every inward as well as outward circumstance, whether it relates to our soul or to our body. It includes every motion of our heart, of our tongue, of our hands and bodily members. It extends to all our actions and words, to the use of all our powers and faculties, and to the manner of using every talent we have received, with respect either to God or to man.

title: Among the children of the devil
english: We have lived our manner of life in the world, even in the world of the ungodly. Not only among the children of God, which would have been, by comparison, a little thing, but among the children of the devil, among those who lie in wickedness, in the wicked one. What a world this is! How thoroughly steeped in the spirit it continually breathes! As our God is good and does good, so the God of this world, and all his children, are evil and do evil, so far as they are permitted, to all the children of God.

Like their father, they are always lying in wait, or walking about, seeking whom they may devour. They use fraud or force, secret tricks or open violence, to destroy those who are not of the world. They are continually warring against our souls, and by old or new weapons, and by devices of every kind, they labor to bring them back into the snare of the devil, into the broad road that leads to destruction.

title: Simplicity
english: We have lived our whole manner of life in such a world, in simplicity and godly sincerity. First, in simplicity. This is what our Lord recommends under the name of a single eye. The light of the body, he says, is the eye. If therefore your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light. The meaning is this. What the eye is to the body, the intention is to all the words and actions. If therefore this eye of your soul is single, all your actions and your manner of life will be full of light, of the light of heaven, of love and peace and joy in the Holy Ghost.

We are simple of heart when the eye of our mind is fixed singly on God, when in all things we aim at God alone, as our God, our portion, our strength, our happiness, our exceeding great reward, our all, in time and in eternity. This is simplicity: when a steady view, a single intention of promoting his glory, of doing and suffering his blessed will, runs through our whole soul, fills all our heart, and is the constant spring of all our thoughts, desires, and purposes.

title: Godly sincerity
english: We have lived our manner of life in the world, second, in godly sincerity. The difference between simplicity and sincerity seems to be chiefly this. Simplicity regards the intention itself. Sincerity regards the carrying out of it. And this sincerity relates not merely to our words, but to our whole manner of life, as described above. It is not to be understood here in that narrow sense in which Saint Paul himself sometimes uses it, for speaking the truth, or for abstaining from guile, from craft and disguise. It is used in a wider meaning, as actually hitting the mark which we aim at by simplicity.

Accordingly, it implies in this place that we do in fact speak and do all to the glory of God. All our words are not only aimed at this, but actually serve it. All our actions flow on in an even stream, uniformly serving this great end. And in our whole lives we are moving straight toward God, and that continually, walking steadily on in the highway of holiness, in the paths of justice, mercy, and truth.

The apostle calls this sincerity godly sincerity, or the sincerity of God, to keep us from mistaking it or confusing it with the sincerity of the heathens. For they also had a kind of sincerity among them, for which they professed no small reverence. He likewise uses the phrase to mark the object and the end of this, as of every Christian virtue, since whatever does not ultimately tend to God sinks among the beggarly elements of the world. By calling it the sincerity of God, he also points out its author, the Father of lights, from whom every good and perfect gift comes down. This is declared still more clearly in the following words: not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God.

title: Not with fleshly wisdom
english: Not with fleshly wisdom. As if he had said: We cannot live in this way in the world by your natural strength or understanding, nor by any knowledge or wisdom acquired by nature. We cannot gain this simplicity, or practice this sincerity, by the force of good sense, good nature, or good breeding. It overshoots all our native courage and resolution, as well as all our rules of philosophy. The power of custom is not able to train us up to this, nor are the most exact rules of human education. Neither could I, Paul, ever reach it, notwithstanding all the advantages I enjoyed, so long as I was in the flesh, in my natural state, and pursued it only by fleshly, natural wisdom.

And yet surely, if any man could, Paul himself might have reached it by that wisdom. For we can hardly conceive of anyone who was more highly favored with all the gifts both of nature and of education. Besides his natural abilities, probably not inferior to those of any person then upon the earth, he had all the benefits of learning, studying at the university of Tarsus, and afterward brought up at the feet of Gamaliel. Gamaliel was the person of the greatest account, both for knowledge and for integrity, in the whole Jewish nation at that time. And Paul had all the possible advantages of religious education, being a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee, trained up in the very strictest sect or profession, distinguished from all others by a more eminent strictness.

And in this he had profited above many others who were his equals in years, being more abundantly zealous of whatever he thought would please God, and, as to the righteousness of the law, blameless. But it could not be that he should reach this simplicity and godly sincerity by that means. It was all lost labor. In a deep, piercing sense of this, he was at length constrained to cry out, The things which were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ. Yes, doubtless, and I count all things but loss, for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord. Philippians 3:7-8.

title: By the grace of God
english: It could not be that he should ever reach this, except by the excellent knowledge of Jesus Christ our Lord, or by the grace of God, another expression of nearly the same meaning. By the grace of God is sometimes to be understood that free love, that unmerited mercy, by which I, a sinner, through the merits of Christ, am now reconciled to God. But in this place it rather means that power of God the Holy Ghost which works in us both to will and to do of his good pleasure.

As soon as ever the grace of God in the former sense, his pardoning love, is shown to our soul, the grace of God in the latter sense, the power of his Spirit, takes place in it. And now we can perform, through God, what was impossible for man. Now we can set our manner of life right. We can do all things in the light and power of that love, through Christ who strengthens us. We now have the testimony of our conscience, which we could never have by fleshly wisdom, that in simplicity and godly sincerity we live our manner of life in the world.

title: The ground of a Christian's joy
english: This is properly the ground of a Christian's joy. We may now therefore readily see how the one who has this testimony in himself rejoices evermore. My soul, he may say, magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior. I rejoice in him who, of his own unmerited love, of his own free and tender mercy, has called me into this state of salvation, in which through his power I now stand. I rejoice because his Spirit bears witness to my spirit that I am bought with the blood of the Lamb, and that, believing in him, I am a member of Christ, a child of God, and an inheritor of the kingdom of heaven.

I rejoice because the sense of God's love to me has, by the same Spirit, worked in me to love him, and to love for his sake every child of man, every soul that he has made. I rejoice because he gives me to feel in myself the mind that was in Christ. That mind is simplicity, a single eye to him in every motion of my heart, power always to fix the loving eye of my soul on him who loved me and gave himself for me, to aim at him alone, at his glorious will, in all I think or speak or do. It is purity, desiring nothing more but God, crucifying the flesh with its affections and lusts, and setting my affections on things above, not on things of the earth. It is holiness, a recovery of the image of God, a renewal of the soul after his likeness. And it is godly sincerity, directing all my words and works so as to serve his glory.

In this I likewise rejoice, yes, and will rejoice, because my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Ghost, by the light he continually pours in upon it, that I walk worthy of the calling with which I am called. I abstain from all appearance of evil, fleeing from sin as from the face of a serpent. As I have opportunity, I do all possible good, of every kind, to all people. I follow my Lord in all my steps, and I do what is acceptable in his sight.

I rejoice because I both see and feel, through the inspiration of God's Holy Spirit, that all my works are done in him, yes, and that it is he who works all my works in me. I rejoice in seeing, through the light of God which shines in my heart, that I have power to walk in his ways, and that through his grace I do not turn from them, to the right hand or to the left.

title: Not a natural joy
english: Such is the ground and the nature of that joy by which an adult Christian rejoices evermore. And from all this we may easily infer, first, that this is not a natural joy. It does not arise from any natural cause. It does not come from any sudden flow of spirits. That may give a passing start of joy. But the Christian rejoices always. It cannot be owing to bodily health or ease, to strength and soundness of constitution. For it is equally strong in sickness and in pain, yes, perhaps far stronger than before. Many Christians have never experienced any joy to be compared with that which then filled their soul, when the body was nearly worn out with pain, or wasted away with pining sickness.

Least of all can it be ascribed to outward prosperity, to the favor of men, or to plenty of worldly goods. For it was then chiefly, when their faith had been tried as with fire, through all manner of outward afflictions, that the children of God rejoiced in him whom, unseen, they loved, even with joy unspeakable. And surely people never rejoiced like those who were treated as the filth and offscouring of the world, who wandered to and fro, in want of all things, in hunger, in cold, and in nakedness, who had trials not only of cruel mockings, but also of bonds and imprisonments, yes, who at last did not count their lives dear to themselves, so that they might finish their course with joy.

title: Not a blind conscience
english: From what has gone before we may infer, second, that the joy of a Christian does not arise from any blindness of conscience, from his not being able to tell good from evil. Far from it. He was an utter stranger to this joy until the eyes of his understanding were opened. He did not know it until he had spiritual senses, fitted to discern spiritual good and evil. And now the eye of his soul does not grow dim. He was never so sharp-sighted before. He has so quick a perception of the smallest things as is quite amazing to the natural man. As a mote is visible in the sunbeam, so to the one who is walking in the light, in the beams of the uncreated Sun, every mote of sin is visible.

Nor does he close the eyes of his conscience any more. That sleep has left him. His soul is always wide awake. There is no more slumber, and no more folding of the hands to rest. He is always standing on the tower, and listening for what his Lord will say concerning him, and always rejoicing in this very thing, in seeing him who is invisible.

title: Not a callous conscience
english: Neither does the joy of a Christian arise, third, from any dullness or callousness of conscience. A kind of joy, it is true, may arise from this, in those whose foolish hearts are darkened, whose heart is callous, unfeeling, dull of sense, and therefore without spiritual understanding. Because of their senseless, unfeeling hearts, they may rejoice even in committing sin. And this they may probably call liberty. It is in fact mere drunkenness of soul, a fatal numbness of spirit, the stupid insensibility of a seared conscience.

On the contrary, a Christian has the most exquisite sensibility, such as he could not have conceived before. He never had such a tenderness of conscience as he has had since the love of God has reigned in his heart. And this also is his glory and his joy, that God has heard his daily prayer.
O that my tender soul might fly the first abhorred approach of evil, quick as the apple of an eye, to feel the slightest touch of sin.

title: Joy in obedience
english: To conclude. Christian joy is joy in obedience, joy in loving God and keeping his commandments. And yet not in keeping them as if we were thereby to fulfill the terms of the covenant of works, as if by any works or righteousness of ours we were to procure pardon and acceptance with God. Not so. We are already pardoned and accepted through the mercy of God in Christ Jesus. Not as if we were, by our own obedience, to procure life, life from the death of sin. This also we have already through the grace of God. He has made us alive who were dead in sin. And now we are alive to God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

But we rejoice in walking according to the covenant of grace, in holy love and happy obedience. We rejoice in knowing that, being justified through his grace, we have not received the grace of God in vain. God has freely reconciled us to himself, not for the sake of our willing or running, but through the blood of the Lamb. We then run, in the strength which he has given us, the way of his commandments. He has girded us with strength for the war, and we gladly fight the good fight of faith. We rejoice, through him who lives in our hearts by faith, to lay hold of eternal life.

This is our rejoicing: that as our Father is working even until now, so we also work the works of God, not by our own might or wisdom, but through the power of his Spirit freely given in Christ Jesus. And may he work in us whatever is well-pleasing in his sight! To him be the praise for ever and ever.

It may easily be observed that the preceding discourse describes the experience of those who are strong in faith. But those who are weak in faith may be discouraged by this. To prevent that, the following discourse may be of use.
